1:
\textbf{(a)} $f(x)=\ln(\tan^{-1}(x^3))$:
\[f'(x)=\frac{1}{\tan^{-1}(x^3)}\cdot\frac{3x^2}{1+x^6},\qquad f'(1)=\frac{3/2}{\pi/4}=\boxed{\frac{6}{\pi}}.\]
\textbf{(b)} $y=(e^{2x}-\ln x)^{10}$:
\[y'=10(e^{2x}-\ln x)^9\Big(2e^{2x}-\frac1x\Big),\qquad y'(1)=10(e^2)^9(2e^2-1)=\boxed{10e^{18}(2e^2-1)}.\]
\textbf{(c)} $y=\frac12x^{\sqrt x}$. Take logs: $\ln y=\ln\frac12+\sqrt x\ln x$, so
\[\frac{y'}{y}=\frac{\ln x}{2\sqrt x}+\frac{\sqrt x}{x}=\frac{\ln x}{2\sqrt x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt x}.\]
At $x=4$: $y=\frac12\cdot4^2=8$ and $\frac{y'}{y}=\frac{\ln4}{4}+\frac12$, so $y'(4)=8\Big(\frac{\ln4}{4}+\frac12\Big)=2\ln4+4=\boxed{4+4\ln2}$.
2:
$y$-intercepts: $x=0$ gives $y^2=\cos0=1$, so $y=\pm1$.

Differentiate $x^2+y^2=\cos x+3xy^3$:
\[2x+2yy'=-\sin x+3y^3+9xy^2y'.\]
At $x=0$: $2yy'=3y^3$, so $y'=\frac{3y^2}{2}=\frac32$ at both points.

At $(0,1)$: \boxed{y=\tfrac32x+1}. \quad At $(0,-1)$: \boxed{y=\tfrac32x-1}.
3:
\[f'(x)=2x-\frac{6x}{x^2+1}=\frac{2x(x^2+1)-6x}{x^2+1}=\frac{2x(x^2-2)}{x^2+1}.\]
Critical numbers in $[-1,3]$: $x=0$ and $x=\sqrt2$ ($-\sqrt2$ is outside). Compare:
\[f(-1)=1-3\ln2\approx-1.079,\quad f(0)=0,\quad f(\sqrt2)=2-3\ln3\approx-1.296,\quad f(3)=9-3\ln10\approx2.092.\]
Absolute maximum \boxed{9-3\ln10} at $x=3$; absolute minimum \boxed{2-3\ln3} at $x=\sqrt2$.
4:
\textbf{(a)} $f(x)=\cos x-x$ is continuous with $f(0)=1>0$ and $f(\pi)=-1-\pi<0$, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem it has at least one zero in $(0,\pi)$. Also $f'(x)=-\sin x-1$, and on $[0,\pi]$ we have $\sin x\ge0$, so $f'(x)\le-1<0$: $f$ is strictly decreasing there and can cross zero only once. So there is exactly one solution.

\textbf{(b)} At $a=\frac{\pi}{4}$: $f(a)=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-\frac{\pi}{4}\approx-0.078291$ and $f'(a)=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-1\approx-1.707107$. Linearization $L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$; setting $L(x)=0$:
\[x=a-\frac{f(a)}{f'(a)}=0.785398-\frac{-0.078291}{-1.707107}\approx\boxed{0.73954}.\]
5:
\textbf{(a)} After 4 min, $V=4(12\pi)=48\pi$ ft$^3$, $r=6$, $h=4$ (check: $\frac{\pi}{3}(36)(4)=48\pi$). Differentiate $V=\frac{\pi}{3}r^2h$:
\[\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{\pi}{3}\Big(2rh\frac{dr}{dt}+r^2\frac{dh}{dt}\Big)\ \Rightarrow\ 12\pi=\frac{\pi}{3}\Big(2(6)(4)\tfrac14+36\frac{dh}{dt}\Big).\]
So $36=12+36h'$, and $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\boxed{\tfrac23\ \text{ft/min}}$.

\textbf{(b)} Each equal side is $s=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$, so $s\,s'=r\,r'+h\,h'$. With $s=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}$:
\[s'=\frac{6(\frac14)+4(\frac23)}{2\sqrt{13}}=\frac{25/6}{2\sqrt{13}}\approx\boxed{0.578\ \text{ft/min}}.\]
6:
\textbf{(a)} Radius \boxed{70\ \text{ft}}; at $t=0$ the location is \boxed{(70,\,74)}; one revolution when $\frac{\pi}{15}t=2\pi$, i.e. \boxed{30\ \text{s}}.

\textbf{(b)}
\[\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}=\frac{\frac{70\pi}{15}\cos(\frac{\pi t}{15})}{-\frac{70\pi}{15}\sin(\frac{\pi t}{15})}=-\cot\Big(\frac{\pi t}{15}\Big).\]
At $t=10$: $-\cot\frac{2\pi}{3}=\boxed{\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}}$.

\textbf{(c)} The far left point is $(-70,74)$, reached when $\frac{\pi t}{15}=\pi$ ($t=15$). There your vertical velocity is $y'(15)=\frac{70\pi}{15}\cos\pi=-\frac{14\pi}{3}\approx-14.66$ ft/s (moving down). The balloon hits a 6-ft head at $t=1$:
\[h(1)=74-A-16=6\ \Rightarrow\ A=52\ \text{ft/s}.\]
$A$ is the wheel's downward speed plus your throw, so your arm threw it at
\[52-\frac{14\pi}{3}\approx\boxed{37.3\ \text{ft/s}}.\]
